opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, the time I spent at a big company was the most important training I've had, but not in the way people usually assume.

At a giant company, you learn what execution really means at scale. When you're shipping millions of units, every small decision gets multiplied: a one-percent defect rate isn't a rounding error, it's tens of thousands of unhappy customers. So you develop a real respect for process, for validation, and for doing the boring things right every single time. I absorbed a lot of that discipline, and I'm grateful for it.

But over time I also felt the other side. In a mature organization, the machine is already built. Your job is mostly to keep it running a bit better. Decisions travel through many layers, and by the time something gets approved, the window that made it exciting may have closed. I remember projects where we knew technically what the right answer was, but it took a year or more just to align everyone. You start to wonder whether your effort is changing the outcome, or just the timeline.

Around that time, I was watching what was happening in China's EV industry, and the pace was just different. Teams were going from concept to a car on the road in a fraction of the time I was used to. Software, electrification, intelligent driving: all of it was being rethought from scratch, not layered onto a fifty-year-old architecture. That was very attractive to me.

So the decision came from both experiences together. The big company taught me how to execute without cutting corners. The new-force automaker offered a place where that execution could matter much more directly, where you could see a decision you made on Monday show up in a product within months. I felt that combination, the discipline from a large organization plus the speed of a startup, was rare and valuable, and I wanted to bring it to a place where it could make a real difference.

Of course, it wasn't all smooth. Some of the habits from a big company had to be unlearned. You can't wait for perfect information, and you can't rely on an army of specialists for every problem. But I think that tension, between rigor and speed, is exactly where a lot of the interesting work happens.

r002.rationale: The response says decisions at the giant company took a long time, then connects that experience to choosing a new-force automaker in China for its faster pace.

fable-5.1.text:
Looking back, the biggest thing I took away from my years at a big company wasn't any particular technology. It was learning what execution actually means at scale. When you're inside an organization like that, you see how a decision travels from a strategy meeting down through dozens of teams, and you see all the places it can die along the way. Alignment, resourcing, the discipline of not changing direction every quarter. Those things sound boring, but they're the real reason a giant company can ship something complex and have it work.

And honestly, that experience made me both more confident and more restless. More confident because I had done it. I knew how to take a vague goal and turn it into a system that ships. But more restless because I could feel the ceiling. In a mature organization, the big bets have mostly been placed. Your job becomes optimizing within a framework somebody else built. You can do very good work, but you're not really deciding what the thing is.

Around that time, I was watching what was happening with electric vehicles in China, and it was obvious the window was open. The new-force automakers were essentially trying to build a car company and a software company at the same time, from zero, in a few years. That is exactly the kind of problem where execution capability is the scarce resource. There's no shortage of ideas or ambition. What's missing is people who have seen how large systems get built without collapsing under their own complexity.

So the decision felt less like leaving something behind and more like finding the place where what I'd learned would actually be the bottleneck. At the giant company, my execution skills were one input among thousands. At a new-force automaker, they could change the trajectory of the whole organization. And there was a personal dimension too. I wanted to be part of building something in China during a moment when the industry was being redefined, rather than reading about it from the outside.

I won't pretend it was a clean calculation. There's real risk. The pace is brutal, the margin for error is thin, and a lot of the process maturity I was used to simply doesn't exist yet. But that's also the point. Bringing that maturity in, without killing the speed that makes a young company dangerous, is the most interesting problem I've ever worked on.

r002.rationale: The response cites limited influence in a mature organization and the opportunity in China’s EV industry, but does not identify slow execution at the giant company as a reason for leaving.

astra-6.text:
Working at a giant company made me appreciate that execution is about much more than having a good idea. You have to turn that idea into a clear goal, get people aligned, and follow through on all the details. It also made me think about where I wanted to put that experience to work.

For me, returning to China and joining a new-force automaker was an opportunity to take greater responsibility for the whole process—from making a decision to seeing its impact on the product. You couldn’t assume the systems or resources would already be there; you had to help build them. That was the attraction: bringing the discipline of a large company into an environment where you also needed to move quickly and keep learning.

r001.rationale: The response says execution involves setting a clear goal and aligning people, but does not distinguish that ability from weak execution at the giant company.

r002.rationale: It describes the appeal of greater responsibility and moving quickly at the automaker, but does not identify slow execution at the giant company as a reason for leaving.

sol-6.1.text:
Working at a giant company taught me that execution isn’t just about moving quickly. It’s about getting people aligned, making clear decisions, and following through across teams. You can have a very good strategy, but if those pieces don’t connect, it won’t turn into a good product.

That experience also made me want to take more ownership—to be closer to the product and see the impact of my decisions. A new-force automaker offered that opportunity. You’re building the organization and its ways of working while developing the car, so the challenges are very immediate.

Returning to China and joining one felt like a chance to apply what I’d learned in a different setting. The important thing was to bring discipline in execution while staying flexible enough to build something new.

r001.rationale: The response discusses alignment and follow-through at a giant company, but does not say Chen Xie could establish shared direction there while perceiving execution as weak.

r002.rationale: It does not identify slow execution at the giant company as a reason for his move; it cites greater ownership and proximity to the product instead.
